source.title: When Does Closeness in Distribution Imply Representational Similarity? An Identifiability Perspective
source.citation: Beatrix M. G. Nielsen et al., 2025
source.authors: Beatrix M. G. Nielsen; E. Marconato; Andrea Dittadi; Luigi Gresele

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests when distributional closeness predicts representational similarity using new distributional and representation measures, and tests a width sweep on synthetic classification tasks.
record.gate_note: Theoretical results and experiments on CIFAR-10 and synthetic data bear directly on distributional and representational similarity. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as results. The CIFAR-10 embedding diagrams and additional plots are described in text but do not provide numeric values in the supplied text.
record.test_reason: The study retrains same-architecture models from different seeds (CIFAR-10 ResNet18 and synthetic MLPs) and measures representational similarity (mCCA, df,g/dSVD). It also reports how that similarity changes with network width. This bears on V3 and, narrowly, on V1 and V4. Its main contribution is identifiability theory linking distributional and representational distance, which uses a new measure aimed at the same question.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that small KL divergence, or near-maximal likelihood, does not guarantee similar representations, and that similarly performing CIFAR-10 retrainings can be dissimilar. They also prove that closeness under their LLV distance bounds their df,g dissimilarity. In synthetic experiments, wider networks give lower mean and variance of dLLV and more similar representations. Whether closeness implies similarity depends on the chosen distances.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops an identifiability-based theory and introduces LLV and PLS-SVD measures; it does not reproduce the original Platonic Representation Hypothesis measurement or its cross-modal experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that LLV values depend on the chosen input and label sets when distributions differ. Their experiments choose pivot and omitted labels and sample input sets to minimize the distance. Conclusions also vary with the distribution and representation measures used (KL, LLV, mCCA, and dSVD).

fits_no_version.finding: For hand-constructed model pairs, dKL falls about four orders of magnitude as unembedding norm grows. Meanwhile mCCA stays near 0, max dSVD near 1, and dLLV near 1.317.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Closeness of output distributions (KL, near-optimal likelihood) does not imply representational similarity.

fits_no_version.finding: The distributional distance dLLV between seed-retrained models falls in mean and spread as width grows. For a CIFAR-10 pair, dKL is about 1.12–1.13 while dLLV is about 1.55, with similar test losses.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Wider networks learn output distributions that are closer under the LLV distance.

record.problems: The main empirical scale evidence is restricted to synthetic classification networks with two-dimensional representations and a fixed task; models are filtered for over 90% accuracy. CIFAR-10 comparisons use low-dimensional representations. Numeric values for the width trends are shown only in figures in the supplied text. The paper's checklist says its plots do not have error bars, although the experimental text describes shaded standard-deviation areas.
record.rows_left_out: No reported result-bearing findings were left out. The CIFAR-10 embedding diagrams and the extra width plots' exact per-width values are figure-only; the text describes their trends but gives no numeric values.

untested.parts: Different architectures, objectives, data or modalities. Real-scale models. Capability beyond width of a 3-layer MLP on a 2D toy task.
Unit-level identity; shared subspaces at realistic representation dimension (all reported CIFAR results use 2D representations).
Stitching, relative representations, unpaired alignment, and mapping loss in realistic models.
No empirical sweep of similarity-measure settings or inputs. Measure invariance differences (mCCA vs df,g) are argued only theoretically (Sec. E.7).
Plateau and the causes of alignment (shared data or objective vs. a common model) are not tested.

missing.what: Difference in test loss vs embedding mCCA across CIFAR-10 seed pairs at representation dimensions 2, 3 and 5 (figure only). It shows small loss gaps alongside low mCCA, and the reverse.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6/V7 labels are dropped. The constructed rows build dissimilarity by design, and KL/LLV are distributional, not representational, measures. Both representation measures (mCCA, dSVD) agree on dissimilarity, so these rows show no metric dependence of convergence. The reader's V7 'challenges' label also had the direction wrong: incomplete alignment would favour V7, not challenge it. All width-trend values are figure-only. Figs 17–18 captions say 'max dLLV' for the right panels while the text says max dSVD. The checklist says the plots have no error bars, but the text describes shaded standard deviations. The authors note the diversity condition may fail for image classifiers with few classes. The study does not cite the Convergent Learning original (it does, ref 37) as a source of its results; it is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Tests width scaling only on synthetic classification networks with a fixed task and architecture family, retaining models above 90% accuracy. Does not test convergence across different architectures, objectives, datasets, or modalities, nor a general increase in capability.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language representation comparison.
Retraining comparisons are made on CIFAR-10 and synthetic data; does not test individual-unit identity or explicitly identify shared subspaces.
Tests linear-similarity measures and a representation dissimilarity measure on embeddings and unembeddings. Does not test stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
No analysis of recurring interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Compares KL, LLV, mCCA, and PLS-SVD-related measures in the reported settings. Does not systematically sweep similarity-measure settings or out-of-distribution inputs.

Shows incomplete alignment despite similar performance and a construction with near-zero KL, but does not isolate whether shared data or objectives cause alignment rather than a common model of reality.
